text: "Dogs" is the fourth episode of the first season of the American comedy-drama television series The Bear, which follows a young chef who returns to Chicago to run his family's sandwich shop after his brother's death.[1] Directed by Christopher Storer and written by Sofya Levitsky-Weitz, the episode premiered on Hulu on June 23, 2022, running for approximately 30 minutes.[1] It centers on multiple storylines: chef Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto and his cousin Richie catering a chaotic children's birthday party at the home of family friend Cicero, while at The Beef restaurant, line cook Tina and sous chef Sydney collaborate on menu development, and pastry chef Marcus innovates with homemade donuts.[1] The episode highlights themes of family tension, workplace dynamics, and culinary creativity amid high-stress environments, contributing to the series' reputation for intense, character-driven narratives.[2]Filmed in Chicago to capture the authentic grit of the restaurant industry, "Dogs" features standout performances from Jeremy Allen White as Carmy, Ebon Moss-Bachrach as Richie, Ayo Edebiri as Sydney, and Liza ColÃ³n-Zayas as Tina, with supporting roles emphasizing interpersonal conflicts and growth.[1] Key scenes include the disastrous party catering job, marked by mishaps like accidentally spiking drinks with medication, and Marcus's meticulous donut experimentation inspired by real-world pastry techniques.[3] The title "Dogs" refers to the hot dogs served at the birthday party.[2] Critically, the episode has been praised for its blend of humor and tension, earning an 8.1/10 rating on IMDb from over 9,000 users and contributing to the season's overall acclaim for its Emmy-winning writing and direction.[1] Episode Overview Synopsis In the episode "Dogs," Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto and Richie Jerimovich handle catering duties for a chaotic children's birthday party at the suburban home of Uncle Cicero (Jimmy), a family friend and local loan shark to whom the restaurant owes money. The event, intended to chip away at their debt, quickly devolves into tension as Carmy navigates awkward family interactions, including relatives mistaking him for his late brother Mikey and dismissing his culinary career as that of a "loser." Richie, stressed and popping anxiety medication, accidentally spills an entire bottle of Xanax into the homemade Ecto Cooler punch bowl, inadvertently drugging the partygoersâincluding Cicero's son and guestsâleading to a sudden wave of sleepy children napping everywhere. When Carmy discovers the mishap and informs Cicero, the uncle reacts with surprising nonchalance, appreciating the unexpected quiet and confirming no one is seriously harmed, which allows the duo to continue serving Chicago-style hot dogs amid banter about local traditions like avoiding ketchup.[2]Meanwhile, back at The Original Beef of Chicagoland, the kitchen staff focuses on prep work during a rare day off from service. Tina Marrero struggles with a new mashed potato recipe under Carmy's instructions but receives hands-on assistance from Sydney Adamu, who demonstrates efficient techniques like knife-peeling and suggests improvements such as a salt bed for seasoning. Their collaboration eases initial friction, with Tina expressing gratitude for Sydney's fair and direct approach, marking a subtle bonding moment in the high-pressure environment.[2]In a quieter subplot, pastry chef Marcus Brooks dives enthusiastically into experimenting with donuts and cakes, inspired by a morning visit to a local bakery and memories of standout flavors. He shares a promising chocolate cake with the team, brainstorming signature items for the restaurant while drawing encouragement from Sydney, highlighting his growing passion and focus amid the group's evolving dynamics. The episode concludes with the catering team cleaning up the subdued party, driving a drowsy Pete (Natalie's husband) home, and returning to the beef stand, where Marcus offers cake slices as a gesture of shared progress.[2] Cast and Crew Main Cast The episode features the core ensemble of The Bear, with performances tailored to the high-pressure catering scenario central to "Dogs." Jeremy Allen White stars as Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto, the talented but overwhelmed chef navigating the demands of the event.[1] Ebon Moss-Bachrach plays Richard "Richie" Jerimovich, delivering comic relief through his exasperated interactions amid the chaos.[1] Ayo Edebiri portrays Sydney Adamu, the ambitious line cook who shares a pivotal moment of collaboration with her colleague.[1] Liza ColÃ³n-Zayas embodies Tina Marrero, the veteran cook whose guidance highlights themes of mentorship in the kitchen.[1] Abby Elliott appears as Natalie "Sugar" Berzatto, providing a subtle family connection in a limited capacity.[1] Supporting roles include Lionel Boyce as Marcus Brooks, focusing on his innovative doughnut preparation, and Matty Matheson as Neil Fak, contributing to the event's logistical frenzy.[1] Guest Appearances Key guest stars include Oliver Platt as Jimmy "Cicero" Kalinowski, the loan shark hosting the party; Chris Witaske as Pete, Natalie's husband who attends the event; and Edwin Lee Gibson as Ebra, appearing in restaurant scenes.[1] Jamie Lee Curtis does not appear in "Dogs" as Donna Berzatto, her recurring role as Carmy's mother reserved for later episodes.[1] The kids' party features several uncredited child extras, with no specific actors highlighted in the episode's billing for those roles.[1] Crew Christopher Storer directed "Dogs," bringing his signature kinetic style to capture the episode's frenetic energy.[1] The teleplay was written by Sofya Levitsky-Weitz, who crafted the script's blend of humor and tension.[1] Among the executive producers, Hiro Murai oversaw the tonal balance, ensuring the episode's mix of comedy and culinary intensity aligned with the series' vision.[1] Joanna Calo served as showrunner and executive producer, contributing to the overall production framework.[4] Background and Context Real-Life Inspirations The episode "Dogs" draws significant inspiration from Chicago's vibrant diner and sandwich shop culture, particularly through Uncle Jimmy's recollection of Carmy's father being motivated to enter the restaurant business after experiencing the theatrical atmosphere at Ed Debevic's.[5] Opened in 1984 by the Lettuce Entertain You Enterprises restaurant group in Chicago's River North neighborhood, Ed Debevic's quickly became iconic for its retro 1950s diner theme, complete with checkered floors, neon signs, and a menu of classic American fare like burgers, milkshakes, pancakes, and skillets.[6] What set it apart was the sassy, interactive service, where costumed waitstaffâoften in poodle skirts or leather jacketsâdelivered insults, songs, and playful banter to patrons, turning meals into entertaining performances that appealed to families and tourists alike.[7] The original location at 640 N Wells Street operated until 2015, when it closed for redevelopment, but the concept was revived in a new Streeterville spot at 159 E Ohio Street in 2021, maintaining the high-energy vibe that captured the spirit of 1980s Chicago hospitality.[8] This real-world establishment's blend of nostalgia and showmanship mirrors the chaotic, character-driven energy of the Berzatto family dynamics portrayed in the series.The Berzatto family's beef stand, The Original Beef of Chicagoland, reflects the city's longstanding tradition of Italian beef sandwich shops, which form a cornerstone of its working-class culinary heritage. Italian beef sandwiches originated in Chicago's Italian-American communities during the early 20th century, evolving from economical ways to feed large crowds at weddings and festivals by thinly slicing roast beef, seasoning it with Italian spices, and piling it on crusty rolls with giardiniera or sweet peppers.[9] These no-frills stands, often family-run and concentrated in neighborhoods like Little Italy and the Near West Side, emphasize quick service, bold flavors, and community ties, much like the gritty, debt-ridden operation inherited by Carmy.[10] Key inspirations include Mr. Beef, a River North staple founded in 1979 that served as the primary real-life model for The Beefâcreator Christopher Storer drew from his time working there, incorporating its authentic sandwich preparation and bustling counter setup into the show's depiction.[5] Other influences appear in the episode's montage of Chicago eateries, such as Johnnie's Beef in Elmwood Park (opened 1961), renowned for its charcoal-grilled sausages and beef dipped in gravy, and Gene & Jude's in River Grove (since 1946), famous for "red hots" topped with sport peppers and fries but no ketchup or seatingâhallmarks of the unpretentious beef stand ethos that underscores the Berzattos' blue-collar roots.[5] Cultural References In the episode "Dogs," a subtle tribute to Chicago native Harold Ramis, the acclaimed director of films such as Ghostbusters (1984) and Caddyshack (1980), appears through character dialogue referencing his legacy as a cornerstone of Chicago comedy.[11] This nod underscores the city's rich comedic heritage, with Ramis's work often celebrating Midwestern humor and underdog stories.Central to the episode's chaotic kids' party scene is Carmy's recreation of Ecto Cooler, a Hi-C fruit punch drink originally launched in 1987 as a promotional tie-in with The Real Ghostbusters animated series, featuring a neon green color and citrus flavor inspired by the franchise's ectoplasm.[12] The beverage, which gained cult status among 1980s and 1990s children, was discontinued in the early 2000s after later rebrandings, including to Shoutinâ Orange Tangergreen in 2001 and Crazy Citrus Cooler in 2006, but saw a limited revival in 2016 to coincide with the Ghostbusters reboot film.[13] In the plot, an accidental spiking of the drink with Xanax mirrors tropes of unsupervised youthful mischief in family-oriented media, amplifying the episode's themes of improvisation under pressure.[14]The episode's soundtrack incorporates culturally resonant tracks that evoke American nostalgia. "Help Me, Rhonda" by the Beach Boys (1965) plays during a moment of familial tension, its harmonious surf-rock style recalling 1960s ideals of domestic harmony and beachside innocence often depicted in period media.[15] Similarly, John Mellencamp's "Check It Out" (1987) underscores scenes of blue-collar Midwestern life, its heartland rock sound nodding to the region's working-class ethos and small-town resilience as portrayed in Mellencamp's broader discography.[16] These selections tie into the episode's Chicago setting, blending pop culture callbacks with local identity. Production Process Development and Writing The writing of "Dogs," the fourth episode of The Bear's first season, was handled by Sofya Levitsky-Weitz, who emphasized comedic relief following the emotional intensity of the prior episode "Braciole," while leveraging her background in television writing to underscore workplace bonding amid the restaurant's high-pressure chaos.[2] Positioned as a seasonal breather, the episode spotlights family ties and team relationships to ease pacing before escalating tensions in later installments, incorporating dark comedic elements such as the accidental Xanax contamination of children's drinks to inject perverse humor into tense scenarios.[17] Showrunners Christopher Storer and Joanna Calo, in collaboration with executive producer and writer Rene Gube, guided the script to equilibrate the series' gritty realism with levity, drawing on Storer's firsthand restaurant line-cooking experience to authentically portray the blend of devastation and deflection in kitchen life.[18] Filming Locations The opening sequence of the episode "Dogs," featuring pastry chef Marcus's subplot, was filmed at Roeser's Bakery, Chicago's oldest family-owned bakery, established in 1911 and located in the Humboldt Park neighborhood. This historic site provided an authentic backdrop for Marcus's visit, where he draws inspiration for his doughnut experiments by observing the bakery's intricate baking techniques and displays.[5]The chaotic children's birthday party at Uncle Cicero's home, central to the episode's catering storyline, was shot at a French country-style estate at 1631 Ridgewood Lane in Glenview, Illinois, a northern suburb of Chicago. The 5,767-square-foot property, with its expansive interiors including a chef's kitchen, sunroom, recreation room, terraces, veranda, antique brick patios, and English gardens, served as both exterior and interior locations, capturing the upscale suburban setting that amplified the episode's comedic tension and family dynamics. Filming spanned three days, allowing the production to utilize the home's natural light and entertaining spaces to enhance visual realism.[19]Interiors of The Original Beef of Chicagoland, including scenes of party preparation, continued to be filmed on a soundstage at Cinespace Chicago Film Studios on the city's West Side. This replica set meticulously recreated the restaurant's gritty, grease-stained environment from the pilot episode onward, with modifications for the episode's catering elements to maintain continuity and authenticity in depicting the kitchen's high-pressure atmosphere.[20] Costuming and Props In the episode "Dogs" of The Bear, costuming choices for key characters emphasize the chaotic contrast between high-pressure kitchen work and suburban catering demands. Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto, played by Jeremy Allen White, wears a checked zip-front jacket from the Danish brand NN.07, specifically the Gael model in a wool-blend fabric, during the catering gig at the children's birthday party. This garment, with its boxy fit and textured pattern, underscores Carmy's stressed and somewhat out-of-place demeanor amid the event's escalating mishaps.[21]Sydney Adamu, portrayed by Ayo Edebiri, appears in kitchen scenes sporting a headscarf as part of her practical uniform, aligning with her role in managing the restaurant back home. While specific designs vary across seasons, her use of vibrant bandanas, such as patterned styles tied to evoke focused energy, highlights her evolving confidence in the culinary environment.[22]Props at the kid's party further amplify the episode's themes of excess and unintended consequences. Carmy prepares a homemade version of Ecto Cooler, a nostalgic Hi-C flavor tied to Ghostbusters, using fresh-cut fruits blended into a punch served from a bowl, which becomes central to a comedic sequence involving accidental sedation. The setup includes basic party elements like a backyard gathering space, reinforcing the suburban overindulgence that clashes with the crew's professional intensity. Donut props sourced from a local bakery appear briefly in related restaurant contexts.[14] Soundtrack and Music The soundtrack for the episode "Dogs" of the FX series The Bear features a curated selection of licensed tracks that enhance its emotional and comedic beats, blending nostalgic pop with contemporary sounds. The episode opens with "One Fine Day" by David Byrne and Brian Eno, accompanying a montage of bakery preparations that sets a whimsical tone for the ensuing chaos.[16] As the party setup unfolds, "Help Me, Rhonda" by the Beach Boys injects levity into the mounting tension among the characters. Later, "Loved by You" by KIRBY underscores a tender bonding moment between Sydney and Tina, providing a soulful contrast to the episode's frenetic pace. The climax builds energy with "Check It Out" by John Mellencamp, amplifying the high-stakes party dynamics.[16]Complementing these needle drops, the original score incorporates tense string arrangements during the Xanax incident to heighten suspense, while upbeat horn sections punctuate comedic beats throughout the narrative. These elements were composed by collaborators of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, who oversee the series' overall scoring and infuse it with electronic and orchestral textures.[23][24]Music supervision for "Dogs" emphasizes a fusion of 1980s nostalgiaâevident in selections like the Beach Boys and Mellencamp tracksâwith modern indie influences, such as KIRBY's contemporary R&B, to mirror the episode's cultural references to retro aesthetics and interpersonal warmth. This approach ties into the series' broader sonic strategy of using music to evoke emotional resonance amid culinary and personal turmoil.[25][23] Culinary Elements Featured Dishes In the episode "Dogs" of the FX series The Bear, the Chicago-style hot dog serves as a central culinary element during a catered children's birthday party, highlighting the city's iconic street food traditions. Prepared with an all-beef frankfurter on a poppy seed bun and topped with yellow mustard, neon-green sweet pickle relish, chopped white onions, tomato wedges, a dill pickle spear, sport peppers, and a dash of celery salt, the dish strictly adheres to the "no ketchup" ruleâa longstanding Chicago custom that sparks comedic tension when the kids demand the condiment, leading to a heated debate among the characters. This preparation underscores the hot dog's role as a symbol of local authenticity, with the episode's catering setup amplifying the cultural debate over proper toppings.[2]Another featured beverage is the homemade Ecto Cooler, a nostalgic recreation of the 1980s Hi-C drink tied to Ghostbusters, prepared as a vibrant green punch for the party. In the plot, Carmy prepares it as a fun, kid-friendly option, evoking 1980s pop culture while unknowingly spiking it with Richie's accidentally misplaced pills, which adds a layer of chaotic humor to the gathering. The drink's appearance pays subtle homage to Chicago native Harold Ramis, co-writer of the original Ghostbusters film, blending culinary creativity with thematic nostalgia.[2][14]Marcus's chocolate cake emerges as an emotional highlight, a multi-layered confection featuring rich chocolate sponge cake filled with airy mousse and crowned with a glossy Valrhona ganache, dramatically unveiled at the episode's close to cap his subplot's arc of dedication and growth. Created by the show's pastry consultant Sarah Mispagel-Lustbader of Chicago's Loaf Lounge, the cake uses high-quality Valrhona cocoa powder and 64% Tainori chocolate, resulting in a decadent, indulgent dessert that becomes a fan-favorite recreation. Its presentation at the party not only showcases Marcus's baking prowess but also ties into brief visuals of his donut experiments, adding to the episode's focus on pastry artistry.[26][27]Tina's experimentation with a new mashed potato recipe represents another key culinary thread, as she collaborates with Sydney on menu development at The Beef, emphasizing iterative creativity in a low-pressure moment.[2] Kitchen Techniques In the episode "Dogs" of The Bear, Marcus Brooks undertakes a meticulous trial-and-error process to develop donuts, beginning with dough preparation influenced by observations at Chicago's historic Roeser's Bakery, known for its traditional methods. Actor Lionel Boyce, who portrays Marcus, drew from personal experiments and staging at bakeries like Tartine in Los Angeles, where he learned to maintain a focused rhythm during long rising periods, emphasizing the time-intensive nature of baking that often exceeds on-screen depictions.[2][28][29]Pastry consultant Sarah Mispagel-Lustbader provided expert guidance for cake assembly scenes in the series, adapting professional layering techniques for dramatic effect, including precise stacking of sponge layers with chocolate mousse dams to prevent overflow and ensure stability. Baking occurs at 350Â°F (177Â°C) for 25-30 minutes per layer, followed by 1.5-2 hours cooling, with the mousse chilling for at least 8 hours before assembly and a brief 15-minute set after icingâelements critical to the emotional resonance of key scenes. Her input, based on her experience at Chicago's Loaf Lounge, prioritized balanced textures, with the multi-component prep highlighting the precision required in high-stakes pastry work.[30][27]During the kid's birthday party catering in "Dogs," the team employs quick-assembly methods for hot dogs and punch to manage time pressure, demonstrating brigade system efficiency through delegated roles: Carmy prepares the homemade punch, while Richie and others grill and top hot dogs with classic Chicago fixings like sport peppers and relish in a coordinated flow. This reflects the hierarchical brigade de cuisine structure, where clear commands and rapid handoffs enable high-volume output, as informed by culinary producer Courtney Storer's oversight to authentically portray chaotic yet streamlined professional catering.[2][31] Themes and Analysis Character Arcs In the episode "Dogs," the dynamic between Carmy Berzatto and Richie Jerimovich evolves through their forced collaboration while catering a family party, exposing deep-seated tensions rooted in grief and differing visions for the restaurant while fostering fleeting moments of camaraderie. As they navigate the chaotic suburban event, their interactions reveal Carmy's internal leadership struggles, particularly his isolation amid familial belittlement, contrasted by Richie's impulsive chaos that inadvertently smooths over conflicts, such as bonding over disdain for Sugar's husband Pete. This partnership not only advances Carmy's arc by highlighting his vulnerability and need for external validation but also underscores Richie's role as a reluctant ally, chipping away at their debt while strengthening their bond under pressure.[2]Sydney Adamu's mentorship of Tina Marrero progresses significantly during their shared kitchen shifts at The Original Beef of Chicagoland, where direct guidance and encouragement build Sydney's confidence as a leader and earn Tina's respect, emphasizing a transfer of generational knowledge in a high-stakes environment. Sydney's straightforward approachâoffering compliments and fair instruction on new recipes like mashed potatoesâhelps Tina adapt to the restaurant's evolving demands, marking a pivotal step in Sydney's growth from newcomer to authoritative figure and Tina's shift from resistance to immersion in modern techniques. This relationship highlights themes of trust and adaptation, with Sydney's persistence suggesting sustained development in their professional rapport.[2]Marcus Brooks's quiet dedication to pastry work stands out amid the episode's frenzy, as his focused experimentation with doughnuts and a chocolate cake illustrates his passion and creative drive, contrasting the surrounding chaos and foreshadowing deeper exploration of his personal arc. Visiting a local bakery for inspiration and immersing himself in the craft without immediate team benefits, Marcus demonstrates resilience and intrinsic motivation, positioning him as a stabilizing force whose skills promise future contributions to the restaurant's transformation. This portrayal advances his character by emphasizing his understated commitment, setting the stage for growth beyond the core kitchen turmoil.[2] Humor and Tone The "Dogs" episode employs a sitcom-like structure centered on a fish-out-of-water premise, where Carmy and Richie navigate a chaotic suburban children's birthday party while catering hot dogs, leading to escalating mishaps that blend slapstick physical comedy with awkward social discomfort. For instance, Richie's debate over ketchup on hot dogs highlights their disconnect from the innocent partygoers, while their improvised arrival with a hot dog-shaped balloon adds visual farce to the unfolding absurdity. This setup draws on classic ensemble comedy tropes, building tension through rapid-fire errors that culminate in unintended chaos, as analyzed in Collider's breakdown of the episode's perverse humor in tense scenarios.[17]Balancing this levity, the episode incorporates dark comedy by framing the accidental drugging of the childrenâvia Xanax-laced punchâas an absurd tragedy that paradoxically restores calm to the event, contrasting sharply with the high-pressure intensity of the restaurant world back at The Beef. Uncle Cicero's wry approval of the sedated kids underscores the Berzatto family's normalized dysfunction, turning potential horror into mordant relief and reflecting the series' willingness to extract laughs from moral ambiguity and familial trauma. Variety highlights this as the episode's key defense of The Bear's comedic credentials, where high-stakes blunders yield black humor without easy resolution.[32]Tonal transitions provide breathing room within the season's relentless stress, shifting from the party's frantic energy to quieter, tender interludes that humanize the characters amid the farce. At the restaurant, Marcus's focused effort on perfecting a pastryâevident in his meticulous preparationâoffers a moment of introspective calm, allowing subtle growth away from the comedic frenzy. These pivots from broad awkwardness to emotional nuance not only relieve narrative pressure but also reinforce the episode's hybrid tone, blending rapid hijinks with poignant undercurrents. Collider notes how such shifts ground the dark laughs in character development, preventing the comedy from feeling detached.[17] Reception Critical Reviews Critics upon the 2022 release of "Dogs," the fourth episode of The Bear's first season, generally applauded its shift to a lighter, more comedic tone amid the series' intense kitchen drama, while offering mixed views on its heavy reliance on Chicago cultural markers.In a recap, Vulture praised the episode for its emotional depth and authenticity in portraying family tensions and character growth, noting that it "delivers heart and grit, which The Bear is never really lacking," particularly through moments of unexpected support at Uncle Cicero's suburban party. However, the same review critiqued the overabundant Chicago referencesâsuch as the nod to director Harold Ramis via a homemade Ecto Cooler drinkâas feeling forced, suggesting they resulted from a "Chicago punch-up" in the script that laid local flavor on too thick.[2]The New York Times thought the Ramis nod was a nice "deep cut" nod to the city's vibe. Audience and Legacy Upon its release in June 2022, the episode "Dogs" generated significant initial audience buzz for its comedic relief amid the series' tense tone, particularly the chaotic children's birthday party scenes where accidentally Xanax-laced Ecto Cooler leads to kids passing out en masse.[33] Viewership metrics for The Bear's first season indicated a surge in engagement, with the episode serving as a lighter entry that contrasted the heavier dramatic arcs and helped propel the show's overall summer breakout success on Hulu, averaging among the platform's most-watched half-hour series.[34]In 2024 retrospective rankings, "Dogs" solidified its status as a highlight of the first three seasons. The Hollywood Reporter placed it third overall, praising its blend of family drama, high comedyâlike the inflatable hot dog fight and Uncle Cicero's anticsâand accessible storytelling that makes it ideal for newcomers.[35]Variety ranked it fourth among the series' top ten episodes, calling it The Bear's strongest rebuttal to claims it's not a comedy, spotlighting darkly hilarious moments such as the Xanax-spiked punch and a guest mistaking Carmy for his late brother.[32]In later reassessments up to 2024, "Dogs"' enduring appeal continued. Vulture's ranking of episodes up to season 3 positioned it highly, noting its charm.[36]Collider included it in its top ten "bangers," lauding the episode's non-restaurant setting and the perverse humor of the sleeping kids as a comedic pinnacle.[37]Esquire ranked it among the best episodes, highlighting its sitcom-like vibes infused with dark twists, balancing party farce with character growth.[38]BuzzFeed echoed this in a roundup of the show's funniest moments, deeming "Dogs" potentially the funniest TV episode in recent memory for its party chaos.[33]The episode's legacy lies in broadening perceptions of The Bear's tonal range, from high-stakes kitchen intensity to absurd family comedy, while inspiring fan discussions on the series' authentic depiction of Chicago's working-class culture and culinary traditions, such as Italian beef and neighborhood catering gigs.[39] This versatility influenced the show's reputation for genre-blending innovation, encouraging recreations of featured elements like homemade Ecto Cooler among enthusiasts.[14]

text: Dogs What is a dog? Domestic dogs evolved from wolves—either grey wolves or another, now-extinct type of wolf—though there is some scientific debate about their exact origin. Genetics suggest that dogs broke off from their wild ancestors between 14,000 and 29,000 years ago and became domesticated through human interactions. There are over 400 dog breeds, but every variation is a member of the same species, Canis lupus familiaris, and all are related to other wild canines, like foxes. Dogs come in all shapes and sizes, ranging from huge Great Danes to tiny teacup Chihuahuas. Dog weights range wildly from 1.8 kilograms (4 pounds) for toy poodles to 104 kilograms (230 pounds) for the largest mastiffs. Humans used simple forms of genetic engineering to breed dogs for specific instincts and characteristics, and the first domestic dogs were likely bred for hunting. Today, many people keep pet dogs for companionship and comfort, though there are still many modern jobs for dogs, from providing services to individuals to sniffing out wildlife crime. Unfortunately, feral dogs can wreak havoc in their local ecosystems, primarily by preying on native wildlife, leading to severe population declines. What is a dog’s scientific name? The scientific name for a dog is Canis lupus familiaris. They are a domesticated subspecies of grey wolves (Canis lupus). There are over 400 distinct dog breeds, but they all fall within the same species. Where do dogs live? Dogs are now found all over the world. Their ancestors, grey wolves, were originally found throughout the northern hemisphere and were the world’s most widely distributed mammal at one point. Evolution The evolution of dogs from grey wolves occurred over thousands of years through a combination of natural selection and human influence. Research shows that the first domesticated wolves occurred between 14,000 and 29,000 years ago. The exact timeline and details of this domestication process are still debated among scientists, as there were likely several unique instances of wolves being domesticated in different parts of the world at different times. Around 20,000 to 40,000 years ago, it is believed that humans and grey wolves started developing a mutually beneficial relationship. Different packs of wolves, in different geographical areas, entered this relationship in different ways. For example, wolves in northern Eurasia likely had a hand in their own domestication by following around nomadic people and eating the remains of animals and other food scraps these people left behind. Over time, a form of natural selection occurred. Wolves that were more tolerant of humans and were less aggressive would have been more likely to thrive in this new environment. As wild animals, it’s unclear exactly how wolves became comfortable sharing space with humans. However, once they did, humans began to breed them, using simple forms of genetic engineering to breed for specific instincts and characteristics. The first dogs were likely bred for hunting, herding livestock, working and towing sledges in the cold, and protection. For example, huskies were bred to withstand cold temperatures, German shepherds to herd livestock, and dachshunds for their ability to chase badgers into burrows. As human societies developed and diversified, so did the roles assigned to dogs, and different breeds emerged based on specific needs and preferences. Selective breeding by humans further accentuated certain physical and behavioral traits, resulting in the wide variety of dog breeds we have today. Dogs as pets Over time, humans bred dogs to serve as companions rather than for working purposes. Nowadays, dogs are popular pets, and there are hundreds of different breeds. Let’s examine the major dog breed groups and their characteristics. - Sporting group: Bred to assist hunters in capturing and retrieving feathered game, these dogs often have thick, water-repellent coats. Sporting breeds include Labrador retrievers and cocker spaniels. - Hound group: Bred to pursue warm-blooded, fast prey while hunting, these dogs are sleek, have long legs, and can run very fast for short bursts. Hound breeds include greyhounds and bloodhounds. - Working group: These dogs developed to assist humans with daily tasks, like pulling sledges and guarding flocks or homes. Working breeds include Great Danes and rottweilers. - Terrier group: Terriers were bred to hunt vermin and rodents underground. They are feisty and short-legged. Terrier breeds include Scottish terriers and bull terriers. - Toy group: Toy dogs were bred for human companionship and are often small enough to fit in your lap. Popular toy breeds include pugs and Chihuahuas. - Herding group: Herding dogs developed for moving livestock like sheep and cattle, with high energy and natural intelligence. Herding breeds include border collies and German shepherds. - Non-sporting group: This group includes everything left over—the dog breeds that don’t fit into the other categories. Some non-sporting breeds include dalmatians and poodles. Having a dog as a pet can provide many benefits, including reducing loneliness and stress, encouraging movement and exercise, and supporting socialization with other dog owners. Plus, having a dog at home has been shown to make you happier. Studies have shown that dogs can raise levels of oxytocin in humans. Dogs with jobs Many dogs today have jobs that range from being used therapeutically to helping law enforcement. Some prominent, and important dog jobs include: - Therapy dogs, who provide emotional support - Search and rescue dogs for humans and animals—during the devastating 2020 Australian bushfires, dogs were used to locate animals that needed to be rescued from the fires. - Medical dogs that can detect diseases, including Parkinson's, diabetes, epileptic seizures, and cancer, using their strong sense of smell - Military and police dogs, who sniff out explosives and find people or evidence—dogs have also been used to stop wildlife crime by harnessing their tracking skills to detect trafficked animals or animal parts. - Guide or support dogs for individuals with blindness and/or other needs Disaster preparedness Our pets rely on us every day for food, shelter, water, and plenty of belly rubs, but in times of emergency, they need our assistance even more. To prepare your dog for a potential disaster you should do things like: - Microchip them and keep your information up-to-date with the microchip database - Get them vaccinated regularly - Get them comfortable with being in a crate or carrier It’s also a good idea to prepare a pet disaster kit, stocked with everything you may need in the case of an emergency. This should include: - Enough food for two or more weeks - Drinking water - A photo of you with your dog - A collar with an ID tag - Medical records - A dog crate or carrier - Food and water bowls - A lead and/or harness - Any medication your dog needs - If needed, a muzzle and/or other safety equipment The threat dogs pose to wild animals In some cases, dogs can pose a threat to wild animals, through predation, outcompeting wildlife for food, interbreeding, and spreading disease. The Global Invasive Species Database notes that feral or wild dogs threaten nearly 200 IUCN Red List-assessed species. One example includes dogs in the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem in East Africa, which can spread canine distemper virus (CDV) to wild animals, affecting silver-backed jackals, bat-eared foxes, and endangered African wild dogs. A closely related virus, also spread by dogs, has also affected lions, hyenas, bat-eared foxes and leopards in the Maasai Mara National Reserve. Feral domesticated dogs and pet dogs let off their leashes also pose a threat to wild animals. A New Zealand study found that just one German shepherd killed an estimated 500 native kiwi birds. In most cases, when domesticated dogs are involved, it’s up to humans to mitigate these risks to prevent harm to endangered or threatened species. Keeping your dogs monitored and on leashes when they go outside is vital for protecting wild animals. FAQs Can dogs see colors? Dogs can see some color, but not in the same way that humans do. Their vision is similar to humans with red-green color blindness because dogs only have blue and yellow cones in their eyes. How often do dogs go into heat? Female dogs go into heat—which means they are ready to reproduce—approximately every six months. It lasts about 18 to 21 days Heat is made up of four distinct stages: - Proestrus, which lasts up to nine days, is when a bloody discharge first appears in a female. In rare cases, this phase can last up to 28 days. Proestrus ends when the female accepts a male partner. - Estrus is the period when the female is sexually receptive and ready to breed. Ovulation occurs 24 hours after the acceptance of the male. As ova survive for up to four days, a female dog can be impregnated by more than one male during this period. - Diestrus comes after estrus when the female does not fall pregnant, a period which is characterised by a state of ‘pseudopregnancy’. - Anestrus is the final and resting state. How long are dogs pregnant? On average, pregnancy in dogs lasts 63 days from conception to birth. How many puppies can a dog have? Dog litter sizes vary by breed. On average, dogs give birth to five or six puppies at once. Litters of between one and 12 puppies are considered within a normal range. Why do dogs howl? Just like the wolves from which they descend, dogs howl to communicate. They might howl to get humans’ attention, communicate with other dogs, express emotions, out of discomfort and pain, or to respond to other noises. Do dogs sweat? Dogs do sweat, mainly through the pads of their paws. While humans sweat to cool down, dogs have other methods for regulating their body temperature. This includes panting, which causes moisture in the airways to evaporate and cool them down, and vasodilation, where blood vessels expand, moving warm blood to the body’s surface so it can be cooled. How many teeth do dogs have? Just like humans, dogs grow two sets of teeth in their lives: puppy teeth and adult teeth. They begin by growing 28 puppy teeth, which start to come in when they’re three to four weeks old. Next, they grow 42 adult teeth, which begin to present between the ages of three to seven months. When do dogs stop growing? Dogs grow at different rates based on their breed and size. Small dogs (up to nine kilograms or 20 pounds) take around 12 months to reach their full size. Medium dogs, who are between nine and 22 kilograms (20-50 pounds), take around 15 months to reach their full size. Large dogs, who weigh 22 to 45 kilograms (50 to 100 pounds), and extra large dogs over 45 kilograms (100 pounds) take 18 to 24 months to reach full size. Why do dogs have whiskers? Dogs use their whiskers to help guide them through their environment. Whiskers are highly sensitive and transmit sensory information to dogs’ brains. They can detect changes in air currents, which then gives dogs information about the size, shape, and speed of nearby objects. Why do dogs lick humans? Dogs lick humans for several reasons, including: - Expressing themselves - Grooming - Bonding - Getting the human’s attention - Soothing themselves - Showing empathy - Because humans taste good to them Our work IFAW has partnered with organizations all around the globe to rescue and rehabilitate dogs impacted by disasters and conflict. Since the war in Ukraine broke out in 2022, IFAW has worked with partners in Ukraine to rescue animals impacted by the war and provide food, emergency medical treatment, and sheltering. One of our partners is the Step Up rehabilitation center, where dogs with war injuries receive medical care and physical therapy. We also provide grants to Nova Ukraine, a Ukrainian charity that supports animals in shelters and works with local rescue centers, including Animal Rescue Kharkiv. Through their work, more than 200 pets were reunited with their families, including after the Kakhovka dam destruction. Similarly, following deadly earthquakes that struck Syria and Turkey in 2023, IFAW assisted in rebuilding animal shelters that cared for local dog and cat populations. In addition, we’ve worked with communities in Playa del Carmen, Mexico, and local organization Coco’s Animal Welfare to build a clinic, stock it with supplies, and establish veterinary protocols. This project helped keep local dogs and cats safe and encouraged the adoption of more than 1,000 homeless animals. Getting these animals off the streets helps deter jaguars, which are wild predators in the area. In the wake of Hurricane Maria in 2017, we sent over 2,000 pounds of dog and cat food to Dominica to help affected families and their pets. Our team also supported animal search and rescue efforts and emergency sheltering following the wildfires in Butte County, California, in 2020. The Northern Dogs Project helps care for dogs in First Nations communities in rural Canada, where settlements live hours away from veterinary care and often have no other option but to cull dog populations. This project, created with local communities, offers veterinary services, culturally relevant education, and real-life solutions for those who would otherwise not have them. We also have undertaken several projects that have trained detection dogs, including koala detection dogs in Australia, who help locate vulnerable animals, and dogs in Benin who were trained to sniff out wildlife crime and trafficking. Video How can you help? Learning about dogs and how they interact with the natural world is important. Dogs may be one of the most common mammals on earth, but they still need our help—as do the natural habitats threatened by feral populations.
